1044.title: John the Baptist's birth (24 June)
1044.hook: six months before Christmas, at midsummer, as days start shortening: he must increase, I decrease
1044.howItsDone: Churches that keep the birth of John the Baptist read Luke's account of his birth and naming, and in some places people mark the eve of the feast with bonfires.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Corpus Christi: bread carried out of the church and down the street. Your line was christ in the streets. Who did you greet on your street? Day one thousand forty-four, and a new week.

John the Baptist's followers are worried, and they come to him with the news. In the King James Bible: "Rabbi, he that was with thee beyond Jordan, to whom thou barest witness, behold, the same baptizeth, and all men come to him." In other words: the crowds are leaving. The man you pointed to is now drawing everyone, and your river bank is getting quiet. To anyone with a following, that could sound like bad news. Attention moving on. Another name on everyone's lips. His followers might expect him to be hurt, or to fight back. What John says instead turns the worry inside out. And the church gives him a feast day for being born. Today, John the Baptist's birth.

John answers with a wedding. "He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled." He casts himself as the best man. The best man's job is not to be the groom. His joy is standing near and hearing the groom happy. Then the line: "He must increase, but I must decrease." Not said through gritted teeth. Said as the fulfillment of his joy. Now the birth. Luke tells it with care. When the angel visits Mary, he tells her that her elderly cousin Elizabeth is expecting too: "this is the sixth month with her." When Mary arrives, "the babe leaped in her womb." When the baby is born, the neighbors expect him to be named after his father, Zacharias, who can't speak. He asks for a writing tablet and writes, "His name is John." Tradition reads Luke's sixth month this way, and the church calendar sets John's birth six months before Christmas. And some readers notice something in the sky. North of the equator, John's day falls just as the long days of midsummer begin to shorten, and Christmas falls just as the short days begin to lengthen. The light itself seems to act out his line: he must increase, I must decrease. In some places, people light bonfires on the eve of the feast. A celebration for a man remembered for stepping aside.

Here's the practice: find someone else's light. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone near you who is doing well right now. A colleague getting noticed. A friend whose thing is working. A sibling who's having a moment. Notice whatever comes up in you, and don't scold it. Then try John's posture: the friend who stands near, hears the good news, and is glad. If you pray, you can thank God for that person's good thing by name. If you don't, just wish it bigger for them, and mean it if you can. The bell holds the time.
Bridegroom. John the Baptist's name for Jesus, calling himself only the friend who rejoices to hear the bridegroom's voice and happily steps back.
Your line: I must decrease. Today, let someone else shine: pass on a compliment, give away the credit, or point to their good work out loud. Day one thousand forty-four.

1045.title: Peter and Paul (29 June)
1045.hook: the rock and the tentmaker, remembered on one day
1045.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican and Lutheran churches keep Peter and Paul together on one feast day, reading of Peter's confession and of Paul's ministry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bridegroom, and the best man who was glad to step back. Your line was I must decrease. Whose good work did you point to? Day one thousand forty-five.

A shared table in Antioch. Peter is eating with gentile believers. Then visitors arrive from James in Jerusalem, and Peter quietly pulls back and keeps himself apart. Paul sees it, and he doesn't take Peter aside for a private word. He writes about it later, in a letter, in the King James Bible: "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed." Face to face, in front of everyone. Two leaders of the young church, disagreeing in public about who gets to sit at the table. And yet the church calendar puts the two of them on the same day, one feast, both names: not Peter's day and Paul's day, but both. Today, Peter and Paul.
screen: `WHO GETS TO SIT AT THE TABLE?`

segments.voice: Start with how different they were. Peter was a fisherman from Galilee named Simon. In John's Gospel, when his brother Andrew brings him to Jesus, Jesus gives him a new name on the spot: "thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone." Later, in Matthew: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." Paul was a different kind of man entirely. He had hunted down Jesus's followers, until a blinding light on the road to Damascus turned him around. He wrote letters, crossed seas, argued in synagogues and marketplaces, and paid his own way with his hands. Acts says of him and his friends, "by their occupation they were tentmakers." The rock and the tentmaker. The one who walked Galilee with Jesus, and the one who met him on a road, after the resurrection. Now the word pillar. It comes from Paul himself, in the same letter where he tells of the row. He describes going up to Jerusalem, where "James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars," gave him "the right hands of fellowship." Shaking hands across a real difference: Peter to his own people, Paul to the gentiles. So the feast doesn't pretend they always agreed. It holds them up side by side, as two pillars holding up one roof. Churches read Peter's place differently. Catholic teaching sees the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor and reads the rock as Peter himself; Orthodox and Protestant Christians understand the rock and Peter's role in other ways. Tradition says both men died in Rome for their faith. And a letter that carries Peter's name calls Paul "our beloved brother."

Here's the practice: bring two different friends to mind. Settle, and breathe. Pick two people you love who are nothing alike. One loud, one quiet. One who plans, one who wings it. Maybe two who'd argue if you put them in a room. Hold the first one in mind, and what they give you that nobody else does. Then the second. If you pray, you can thank God for each of them by name. If you don't, just be grateful, one at a time, and notice how both of them hold up something in your life. The bell holds the time.
Cephas. The name Jesus gave Simon, meaning a stone, later called Peter, who together with Paul the tentmaker is remembered on one feast as two pillars.
Your line: two pillars. Today, tell one of those two different friends, in a message or out loud, one specific thing you're grateful for. Day one thousand forty-five.

1046.title: Mary Magdalene (22 July)
1046.hook: the apostle to the apostles now has a full feast day
1046.howItsDone: On Mary Magdalene's day, churches that keep it read John 20's garden scene; the Catholic Church keeps it as a feast, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cephas: a fisherman and a tentmaker, once at odds, on one feast. Your line was two pillars. Which friend did you thank? Day one thousand forty-six.

Long loose hair, a jar of ointment at her elbow, eyes lifted, sometimes a skull on the table beside her. In some old paintings, that woman is Mary Magdalene, the weeping sinner. It's a powerful picture. But the Gospels don't paint it. They never call her a prostitute. What they do give her is something else entirely: a job. She's sent with a message, and the people she carries it to are the apostles themselves. That's why one of her old titles sounds like a riddle: the apostle to the apostles. Today, Mary Magdalene.

Start with Luke. He introduces her among the women traveling with Jesus: "Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils." Healed, then. Not a sinner in the text: someone set free. He says these women "ministered unto him of their substance": they paid for the mission out of their own money. When Jesus is crucified, John places her at the cross. And on Easter morning, in John's Gospel, she's alone at the tomb, crying, until the risen Jesus calls her by name and she knows him. Then the part that's easy to skip. He doesn't let her hold on. He gives her an errand: "go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God." And she goes. "Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the LORD, and that he had spoken these things unto her." In John, she's the one who tells them, before Jesus appears to the others that evening. So where did the sinner come from? Over time, some Western preaching merged her with other women in the Gospels: the unnamed woman who weeps on Jesus's feet in Luke, and Mary of Bethany. The texts never join them. Orthodox Christians, who didn't take up that merging, honor her as equal to the apostles. The Catholic Church now keeps her day as a full feast, and uses that old title for her: apostle to the apostles. Different churches, one thing in common. The first words of Easter, in John, travel through her.
screen: `HEALED, NOT A SINNER IN THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a woman's witness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who told you something true that changed things. A grandmother, a teacher, a friend, a nurse, a stranger on a bad day. Maybe someone who wasn't believed at first. Remember what she said, and how she said it. If you pray, you can thank God for her by name, the way the church remembers Mary Magdalene by name. If you don't, just thank her in your mind, and let her words be heard properly this time. The bell holds the time.
Mary Magdalene. Healed and sent, the woman at the tomb who carried the news of Easter to the apostles, remembered with a feast of her own.
Your line: she told them first. Today, when a woman tells you something that matters, give her your full attention, and if it's hers, give her the credit out loud. Day one thousand forty-six.

1047.title: The Transfiguration (6 August)
1047.hook: the mountain of light, on the same date as Hiroshima's bombing
1047.howItsDone: Orthodox, Catholic and some Protestant churches keep the Transfiguration on the sixth of August with readings of the mountain story, and some churches join it with prayers for peace because it shares the date of the Hiroshima bombing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene, sent from an empty tomb with news. Your line was she told them first. Whose witness did you honor? Day one thousand forty-seven.

Three fishermen are climbing behind their teacher, up a high mountain, apart from everyone. Peter, James and John. Somewhere near the top, the man they have been following changes in front of them. His face shines like the sun. His clothes go white as light. Two figures from the old stories are standing there talking with him. And Peter, who Mark says did not know what to say, offers to build some shelters. The church remembers that mountain on the date in today's title, the sixth of August. In a later century, that same date became the day an atomic bomb fell on the city of Hiroshima. One date, two lights. Today, The Transfiguration.

Matthew, Mark and Luke all tell this story. Here is Matthew, in the King James Bible: Jesus "was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light." Transfigured means his form changed. Not a costume, not a trick of the sunset. Then Moses and Elijah appear, the King James spells it Elias, talking with him. Some readers hear the law and the prophets in those two figures, standing beside Jesus. Peter blurts out: "Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias." He wants to keep the moment, to pitch a tent around it. Before he finishes, a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him." The disciples fall on their faces, terrified. And then a quiet moment. Jesus comes and touches them, and says, "Arise, and be not afraid." They look up, and Matthew says they "saw no man, save Jesus only." Then they walk back down the mountain, into ordinary need. Orthodox churches keep this feast, and Catholic and some Protestant calendars keep it too. And the date carries a second light now. On the day the church reads about a light that ends with, be not afraid, a light that burns was loosed on a city and made a whole city afraid. Some churches mark both together, with prayer for peace. The story doesn't make that second light smaller. It just stands beside it.
screen: `HIS FACE DID SHINE AS THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for peace, or hold it in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place where people are afraid tonight because of war. Don't search for the worst image. Just name the place. Then bring to mind Jesus touching his friends on the mountain, and the words, arise, and be not afraid. If you pray, you can offer Jesus's own words from the Sermon on the Mount: blessed are the peacemakers. If you don't, just hold that place, and the people in it, quietly, for the length of the sit. The bell holds the time.
The Transfiguration. The moment on the mountain when Jesus's face shone like the sun, and a voice said, hear ye him. Kept on the sixth of August, the same date as the bombing of Hiroshima.
Your line: two lights. Today, when you switch on a light, let it remind you of the mountain, and of one place that needs peace. Day one thousand forty-seven.

1048.title: Mary's falling asleep (15 August)
1048.hook: Orthodox keep the Dormition, Catholics the Assumption; many Protestants simply honor Mary as a faithful disciple
1048.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians keep the Dormition of Mary in August, and Catholics keep the Assumption on the fifteenth; some Protestant churches keep a festival of Mary, and others simply remember her as a faithful disciple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Transfiguration, a mountain of light on a date that also holds a darker one. Your line was two lights. Where did a light remind you to pray or hope for peace? Day one thousand forty-eight.

Here is an Orthodox icon. A woman lies on a bier, eyes closed, hands folded. The apostles crowd around her, some bending close, some weeping. Behind the bier stands Jesus, in light. And in his arms he holds a tiny figure wrapped in white, like a newborn. It's her soul. At the start of the Gospels, she carried him as a baby. In this picture, he carries her. The woman is Mary, the mother of Jesus. Orthodox Christians call this moment her falling asleep. Today's word: Dormition.
screen: `AN ICON: A WOMAN ON A BIER.`
`JESUS HOLDS HER SOUL LIKE A CHILD.`
`SHE CARRIED HIM. NOW HE CARRIES HER.`

segments.voice: Scripture follows Mary to a last scene, and then goes quiet. In Luke, her answer to the angel ends in a yes: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." At the cross, in John's Gospel, Jesus gives her into a disciple's care: "Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." The last time Acts names her, she is praying with the apostles: "Mary the mother of Jesus." After that, silence. The New Testament never tells how her life ended. So the churches have three ways of keeping this day, and it's fair to name each one plainly. Orthodox Christians keep the Dormition. Dormition means falling asleep. The New Testament can speak of the faithful dead as sleeping; of Stephen, stoned to death in Acts, the King James says simply, "he fell asleep." The Orthodox tradition holds that Mary truly died, surrounded by the apostles, and that her Son received her soul, as the icon shows, and that her body too was then taken up to heaven. Catholics keep the fifteenth of August as the Assumption. Catholic teaching holds that at the end of her earthly life, Mary was taken up, body and soul, into the glory of heaven. Protestants who don't hold either as a teaching give a plain reason: scripture doesn't tell the story. They honor her as Luke does, as the faithful disciple who said yes and kept saying it, all the way to the cross and the upper room. Some keep the day as a plain festival of Mary. Three churches, three ways. What they share is the woman in Luke who said, "all generations shall call me blessed," and a sense that the one who carried Jesus was not forgotten by him.

Here's the practice: honor a faithful mother. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who carried someone: a mother, a grandmother, a foster mother, an aunt, a neighbor who raised half the street. She may be living or she may have died. Think of one specific thing she did, again and again, without applause. A packed lunch. A light left on. If you pray, you can thank God for her by name. If you don't, just hold her in mind with thanks. If she has died, you might picture her, the way the icon does, being carried now. The bell holds the time.
Dormition. The falling asleep of Mary, the Orthodox name for the end of her earthly life. Catholics keep the feast as the Assumption.
Your line: she fell asleep. Today, thank one woman who carried you, in a message, a call, or a quiet word if she's gone. Day one thousand forty-eight.

1049.title: Harvest festival
1049.hook: churches fill with produce, loaves and tins for food banks
1049.howItsDone: Churches and schools hold harvest festivals when the crops are in, decorating the church with produce and bread, singing harvest hymns, and collecting tins and packets for food banks or local charities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dormition, and three ways the churches remember Mary. Your line was she fell asleep. Which woman who carried you came to mind? Day one thousand forty-nine.

A marrow the size of a small dog is lying across the front of the altar. Next to it, a basket of apples, a sheaf of wheat tied with string, a loaf baked in the shape of a wheatsheaf, and a pyramid of tinned tomatoes and baked beans leaning slightly to the left. A child walks up the aisle holding a single carrot as if it were a crown. The church smells of bread and earth. On Monday, the tins will go in a van to the food bank. This is the harvest festival, and a harvest hymn sings that all good gifts around us are sent from heaven above.

Harvest festival isn't a single date in the church calendar. Churches, schools and villages hold it when the crops are in, often on a Sunday in the autumn. But the idea under it is old, and it runs through the Bible. The Psalms sing it to God: "Thou crownest the year with thy goodness." The year has a crown, and the crown is food. The letter of James puts it plainly: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights." The hymn's line, all good gifts, echoes it. The food on the altar is a way of saying: we didn't make this from nothing. Sun, rain, soil, seed, and a lot of other people's work came first. Now the second turn, and it's just as old. The law of Moses tells farmers not to strip their fields bare. In the King James Bible: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." And if a farmer forgets a sheaf in the field, he's told not to go back for it: "it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow." The edges of the field belonged, by law, to the people with no field. That's why the tins matter. The old law built sharing into the harvest itself. The tins of beans are the corners of the field, in a supermarket age. So the harvest festival does two things at once. It looks up, in thanks. And it looks across, to the neighbor whose cupboard is empty.

Here's the practice: bring food to share. Settle, and breathe. Picture your own kitchen, the cupboard, the fridge, the shelf. Walk along it in your mind and notice what's there. Then pick one thing, a tin, a packet, a jar, that you could give away this week, to a food bank, a collection box, a neighbor. Choose something you'd be glad to eat yourself. If you pray, you can give thanks for the people whose work put it on your shelf. If you don't, just hold them in mind: the grower, the picker, the driver. The bell holds the time.
Harvest festival. A church's thanksgiving for the crops, when the altar fills with food, and much of the food goes to people who need it.
Your line: all good gifts. Today, put one tin or packet aside to give away, and before you eat, notice one person whose work is on your plate. Day one thousand forty-nine.

1050.title: Holy Cross Day (14 September)
1050.hook: the cross honored as a sign of victory, not only suffering
1050.howItsDone: On Holy Cross Day, Orthodox churches lift up a cross for the faithful to venerate, and Catholic and some Protestant churches read the scriptures of the cross; Christians in several traditions mark themselves with the sign of the cross in prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harvest festival, with tins on the altar and corners of the field left for others. Your line was all good gifts. What did you put aside to give? Day one thousand fifty.

"God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Paul wrote that to the churches in Galatia, and it's a strange sentence. Glory, in a cross. In Paul's world, a cross was how Rome put people to death, and the letter to the Hebrews speaks of its shame. It was not a thing to boast in. And yet people now trace it on their foreheads, raise it over altars, and hang it round their necks. One day in the church year is set apart to honor the cross itself, not as a defeat but as a victory. Today, Holy Cross Day.

Good Friday looks at the cross with grief. Holy Cross Day looks at it with something closer to wonder. Orthodox Christians call it the Exaltation, or the Elevation, of the Cross: a cross is lifted high in church, and people bow before it. Catholics and some Protestant churches keep the day too. The story behind it is a tradition, not scripture: tradition says that Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine, searched in Jerusalem for the cross of Jesus, and that a church was built at the place. The Bible doesn't tell that story. But it does give the feast its turn of thought. In John's Gospel, Jesus says, "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me." Lifted up: the same act is execution and exaltation at once. Then there's another picture. Peter's first letter says Jesus "bare our sins in his own body on the tree." A tree. That word sends some readers back to the beginning of the Bible, to the garden, where Genesis places "the tree of life also in the midst of the garden," and then forward to the very end, where Revelation shows the tree of life again, by a river, and says "the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations." Old hymns and sermons put those pages together. They sing of the cross as a tree: the dead wood that became the tree of life. A tree in a garden at the start, a tree on a hill in the middle, a tree by a river at the end. That's why the day can be joyful. Christians don't forget the suffering. They honor the cross as the place where, they say, death lost.
screen: `A TREE AT THE START AND THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make the sign of the cross, or bow your head. Settle, and breathe. If it's part of your practice, trace the cross slowly, forehead, chest, one shoulder, then the other, the way your church does it, and let it take a full breath. If it isn't, simply bow your head, the way people bow before the lifted cross. Then rest there. Hold one thing in your life that feels like dead wood. Don't fix it. Just hold it, and let the picture of a tree with healing leaves sit beside it. The bell holds the time.
